stories.title: Google launches the Gemini Decisions API and Gemini Decision 1, a model that scores up to 1,000 yes/no, choice and rubric questions about one multimodal input (text, images, audio, video, PDFs up to 256K tokens) in a single forward pass, without generating text: 150-250 ms end to end, $0.10 per million input tokens, output free; Google says it is best calibrated on its benchmark suite and ~5x cheaper than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite; live on Vercel AI Gateway the same day
stories.h: Google ships Gemini Decision 1, a model that decides instead of writing
stories.ticker: Google launches Gemini Decision 1: calibrated yes/no and choice scores in one pass, $0.10/M input, no output fee
stories.body:
Google DeepMind launched the Gemini Decisions API, powered by a new model, Gemini Decision 1 (gemini-decision-1). Instead of writing an answer token by token, it scores the options you give it in a single forward pass and returns probabilities and confidence scores. One request can carry one input of text, images, audio, video or PDFs (up to 256K tokens) plus up to 1,000 independent questions of three kinds: yes/no, choice and rubric scores. Google quotes 150-250 ms end to end, $0.10 per million input tokens and no output charge, says it leads its benchmark suite with the lowest calibration error, and says it is nearly 5x cheaper than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite on that suite. Vercel's AI Gateway listed it the same day. Simon Willison notes the API copies TypeSafe's Jev almost exactly (Google now joins Jev and OpenAI's decision model); Jev stays cheaper at 4.2 cents per million but handles only text.

So what: decision models are becoming a standard building block. For banks they fit routing, policy checks, document triage and fraud flags, where a calibrated probability and a fixed latency matter more than prose. Three vendors now sell the same shape of API, so switching costs are low.
stories.chip: Checked on Google's launch post and Vercel's changelog; comparison with Jev from Simon Willison
stories.short: Google launched Gemini Decision 1, a model that answers up to 1,000 yes/no, choice or scoring questions about one input (text, images, audio, video or PDF) in a single pass instead of writing text. It returns calibrated probabilities in 150-250 ms for $0.10 per million input tokens, with no output charge.

stat.label: per million input tokens, output free

stories.title: Deutsche Bank launches its crypto custody service for institutional and corporate clients in Europe: Bitcoin, Ether and stablecoins (USDC, EURC, AllUnity EURAU), with the bank holding wallets and keys under a BaFin-supervised MiCA registration dated 12 Oct; it also signs an MoU with DWS on tokenised money-market funds, crypto ETCs and stablecoins
stories.h: Deutsche Bank switches on crypto custody for institutions
stories.ticker: Deutsche Bank launches crypto custody for institutions: BTC, ETH, USDC, EURC
stories.body:
Deutsche Bank launched its digital-asset custody service on Wednesday for institutional and corporate clients, Cointelegraph reports from an announcement shared with it (Reuters also reported the launch). Clients can store and transfer Bitcoin, Ether and selected stablecoins (USDC, EURC and AllUnity's EURAU); the bank manages the wallets and private keys. Its entry in the EU's MiCA register for custody and transfer is dated 12 October, with BaFin as supervisor. The bank also signed a memorandum of understanding with its asset manager DWS to explore tokenised money-market funds, crypto exchange-traded commodities and stablecoins. It first announced the plan on 16 September.

So what: Germany's largest bank now holds crypto for clients under MiCA. That makes custody a standard bank product in Europe, and puts pressure on rivals to offer it, and on crypto-native custodians on price.
stories.chip: Checked on Cointelegraph (citing the bank's announcement); the September plan on Bloomberg Law
stories.short: Deutsche Bank has switched on crypto custody for institutional and corporate clients in Europe. They can hold and move Bitcoin, Ether, USDC, EURC and EURAU, with the bank managing keys under its MiCA registration. It also plans tokenised money-market funds and stablecoin work with DWS.

stat.label: assets at launch: BTC, ETH and three stablecoins

stories.title: United Airlines bans third-party personal AI agents (such as Meta's Muse and OpenAI's agents) from booking or managing flights for travellers, citing credential-sharing risk, unintended purchases or MileagePlus use, and federal rules such as in-person hazardous-materials confirmation at check-in; it will block them on its own platforms and via travel agencies and aggregators
stories.h: United Airlines blocks AI agents from booking flights for customers
stories.ticker: United Airlines bans personal AI agents from booking flights
stories.body:
United Airlines said it is banning third-party personal AI agents from making reservations for travellers, CBS News reports (the NYT and The Information also covered it). United says sharing account credentials with such assistants can expose sensitive data and lead to unintended purchases, account changes or use of MileagePlus miles, and that an agent checking someone in could breach federal rules, such as travellers confirming in person that bags hold no banned items. It will restrict access on its own platforms and indirectly through travel agencies and aggregators, and is updating its booking terms. An analyst told CBS United does not want another powerful intermediary between it and its customers.

So what: the first big merchant to shut the door on consumer agents. Banks and card networks building agent payments (agent tokens, agentic checkout) now face merchants who want to decide which agents may transact, which turns agent identity and liability into a commercial negotiation.
stories.chip: Checked on CBS News
stories.short: United Airlines is banning personal AI agents such as Meta's Muse from booking or changing flights for customers, on its own sites and through travel agencies. It cites shared passwords, unintended purchases and miles use, and federal check-in rules. It is the first big merchant to block consumer agents outright.

stat.label: major airline to ban booking agents

stories.title: British inference-chip start-up Fractile raises a $720M Series C led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint, backed by the UK Sovereign AI Fund, at over £5B (reported ~$7B); its chips stack DRAM directly on each compute die to break the memory-capacity-versus-speed trade-off for long agent workloads, with its own ML compiler
stories.h: Fractile raises $720m to stack memory on AI inference chips
stories.ticker: UK chip start-up Fractile raises $720M at ~$7B for memory-stacked inference chips
stories.body:
Fractile, a London start-up building chips for running AI models (inference), raised a $720 million Series C led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint, with backing from the UK's Sovereign AI Fund, TechCrunch reports. The UK government put the valuation at over £5 billion; the FT and a Reuters source say about $7 billion. The product: after a pivot, Fractile stacks ordinary DRAM directly on top of each chip to avoid the usual trade-off between memory capacity and speed, which bites when agents run long chains of tasks on big models, and it ships its own compiler to schedule models on the hardware. Sifted had first reported the £540m raise.

So what: inference cost is where AI spending is heading, and memory, not maths, is the bottleneck. A credible non-Nvidia design with sovereign backing gives buyers, including banks running models in-house, another future supplier. It ships nothing in volume yet.
stories.chip: Checked on TechCrunch; valuation figures are the UK government's and the FT's
stories.short: London's Fractile raised $720 million, valuing it at about $7 billion, with UK sovereign-fund backing. Its inference chips stack ordinary DRAM directly on each chip so large models can run long agent tasks without the usual memory-speed trade-off. It is among the best-funded challengers to Nvidia for inference.

stories.title: Huntress tracks an active campaign abusing cloud-hosted ConnectWise ScreenConnect: 6 managed service providers compromised and 286+ endpoints at 47 organisations, with attackers using Run Command to push rogue remote-access clients and a possible reverse pivot onto MSP technicians' machines; ConnectWise is investigating and tells partners to avoid interactive sessions with possibly compromised devices
stories.h: Hackers hijack ScreenConnect to reach dozens of MSP customers
stories.ticker: Active ScreenConnect campaign: 6 MSPs, 286+ endpoints, 47 organisations hit
stories.body:
Security firm Huntress is tracking an active campaign, which began around 17:47 UTC on 11 November, against cloud-hosted ConnectWise ScreenConnect instances used by managed service providers (MSPs), BleepingComputer reports. At last count: 6 compromised MSPs and 286+ endpoints across 47 organisations, and rising. Attackers use ScreenConnect's Run Command feature to install their own remote-access clients on customers' machines. Huntress also warns of a possible reverse pivot: compromising a technician's workstation when they open a session to an infected device; it is unclear whether that uses a vulnerability. ConnectWise confirmed it is investigating and told partners to avoid interactive remote sessions with potentially compromised devices. The same week, N-able pulled its N-central RMM offline after 33 alleged zero-days were published.

So what: outsourced IT is a direct path into regulated firms. Banks and insurers should ask their MSPs today whether they use cloud ScreenConnect, what was run on their endpoints since 11 November, and pause interactive sessions until ConnectWise reports.
stories.chip: Checked on BleepingComputer (Huntress figures, ConnectWise statement)
stories.short: Attackers are abusing cloud-hosted ConnectWise ScreenConnect to plant their own remote-access tools: Huntress counts 6 compromised managed service providers and 286+ machines at 47 organisations, still rising. ConnectWise is investigating and tells partners to avoid live sessions with suspect devices. Firms using outsourced IT should check now.

stories.title: N-able takes hosted N-central offline and ships Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) covering seven CVEs after researcher Sean Bales publishes 'Able2Shell': 33 alleged zero-days with proof-of-concept code and four exploit chains to code execution (two as root, one credential-free); the fix disables built-in remote control until a later update
stories.h: N-able disables N-central remote control after 33 zero-days go public
stories.ticker: N-able patches N-central after 33 published zero-days; remote control disabled for now
stories.body:
Researcher Sean Bales published 'Able2Shell' on 9 November: 33 alleged zero-days with proof-of-concept code in N-able N-central, a remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform used by MSPs, including four exploit chains to code execution, two as root and one needing no credentials. N-able took hosted N-central offline as a precaution, told on-premises customers to stay offline until patched, and on 10 November shipped Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26), a critical release covering seven CVEs (XXE, OGNL injection, privilege escalation, XSS, SSRF and path-traversal RCE). It disables built-in remote control until a future fix, Infosecurity reports. Hosted environments are back online.

So what: two of the main tools MSPs use to run client IT were hit in the same week. Any firm whose IT provider runs N-central on premises should confirm Hotfix 2 is installed and that agents and probes were updated.
stories.chip: Checked on Infosecurity Magazine; CVE numbers from N-able's release notes as quoted there
stories.short: A researcher published 33 alleged zero-days in N-able's N-central IT management platform, with working exploit code. N-able took its hosted service offline, then shipped a hotfix for seven CVEs that switches off built-in remote control for now. On-premises customers were told to stay offline until patched.

stories.title: CoreWeave shares jump ~10% after Q3 revenue of $3.66B beats forecasts and management signals an end to heavy borrowing, lifting battered AI-infrastructure stocks and the S&P 500 and Nasdaq on 11 Nov; it then fell 4% after hours on the Nvidia board report
stories.h: CoreWeave results lift AI stocks after a week of selling
stories.ticker: CoreWeave +10% on Q3 revenue of $3.66B; AI stocks rally before Nvidia slides after hours
stories.body:
CoreWeave, which rents out Nvidia-based AI computing, rose about 10% on Wednesday after third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion beat expectations and management signalled it was done piling on expensive debt, Crypto Briefing reports; the WSJ and Economic Times credit CoreWeave with lifting the S&P 500 and Nasdaq. The bounce came less than a week after a historic AI-stock selloff (WSJ). After the close, CoreWeave fell more than 4% as Nvidia slid on the board report (Business Insider). Techmeme also relays a report that CoreWeave plans an investment-grade loan of $4B+ as soon as next week (not checked).

So what: AI-infrastructure credit has been the market's worry (CoreWeave bonds yielded over 16% last week). Better numbers help, but the after-hours reversal shows how much the whole trade still hangs on Nvidia.
stories.chip: Checked on Crypto Briefing and Business Insider; index moves from WSJ and ET headlines
stories.short: CoreWeave shares jumped about 10% after third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion beat forecasts and it signalled an end to heavy borrowing, lifting AI stocks and US indexes on Wednesday. The relief was brief: CoreWeave fell 4% after hours when reports said Nvidia's board might remove its CEO.

stories.title: SoftBank books a ¥597.2B ($3.7B) writedown after cancelling gas-turbine orders it placed to power US AI data centres, helping push it to a ¥1.12T ($7B) net loss for its fiscal second quarter
stories.h: SoftBank writes off $3.7bn on gas turbines it ordered for AI
stories.ticker: SoftBank writes off $3.7B on cancelled AI data-centre turbine orders; Q2 net loss $7B
stories.body:
SoftBank Group took a ¥597.2 billion ($3.7 billion) writedown after cancelling gas-turbine orders it had placed to power AI data centres in the United States, Crypto Briefing reports; The Information and Tom's Hardware also covered it. The charge helped drive a ¥1.12 trillion ($7 billion) net loss for the fiscal second quarter. Tom's Hardware notes it came days after SoftBank denied a claim by Elon Musk about its turbine orders.

So what: the AI power rush produced a turbine queue, and the first big over-order is now a loss. Lenders to data-centre projects should check how much of a sponsor's power plan rests on reservations that can be cancelled or resold.
stories.chip: Checked on Crypto Briefing; The Information and Tom's Hardware seen as headlines
stories.short: SoftBank wrote off $3.7 billion after cancelling gas turbines it had ordered to power US AI data centres, helping drive a $7 billion quarterly net loss. It is the first large loss from the rush to lock up power equipment for AI.

stories.title: MSCI's November index review removes Strategy (MSTR), the largest corporate bitcoin holder, from the MSCI USA Index (and so MSCI World and ACWI) at the close on 30 Nov after a new screen classes it as a non-operating issuer; Metaplanet, Yellow Cake, Skel and Upexi are also cut
stories.h: MSCI drops Strategy from its indexes as a bitcoin holding company
stories.ticker: MSCI removes Strategy (MSTR) from USA, World and ACWI indexes from 30 Nov
stories.body:
MSCI will remove Strategy (MSTR) from the MSCI USA Index at the close on 30 November, which also takes it out of MSCI World and ACWI, after a new screen classified it as a non-operating issuer, Bitcoin Magazine reports from MSCI's November 2026 index review; Cointelegraph confirms. Japan's Metaplanet, uranium holder Yellow Cake, Iceland's Skel and micro-cap Upexi are also deleted. All five were already flagged on MSCI's potential-impact list built on 30 September data.

So what: index funds that track MSCI benchmarks must sell by month-end, removing a steady source of demand for the biggest bitcoin treasury company. It also sets a precedent: holding crypto as the main business now counts as not operating.
stories.chip: Checked on Bitcoin Magazine (citing MSCI's review lists); Cointelegraph headline
stories.short: MSCI will drop Strategy, the largest corporate bitcoin holder, from its USA, World and ACWI indexes on 30 November after classing it as a non-operating company. Funds tracking those indexes must sell. Metaplanet and three other asset-holding companies are also being cut.

stories.title: AWS releases AWS Emulator, a free local emulator of 200+ AWS services whose every line was written by thousands of autonomous AI agents that write tests, find issues and fix code without human review; source is on GitHub under CC0 and updated continuously
stories.h: AWS ships an emulator written entirely by AI agents, unreviewed by humans
stories.ticker: AWS Emulator: local emulator of AWS services, 100% written by autonomous agents, CC0
stories.body:
AWS released AWS Emulator, a local emulator of AWS services that it says was 100% written by autonomous AI agents. In a post, senior principal engineer Matthew Goldberg says thousands of agents write tests, find issues and fix code without human review; the source is on GitHub under a CC0 licence and is constantly updated. GeekWire, via Techmeme, says it simulates 200+ services and that the team has not written or reviewed any of the code. It drew 626 points on Hacker News.

So what: a hyperscaler is shipping software no person reviewed, which pushes the question of how to trust agent-written code from theory into practice. Teams can use it to test AWS workloads offline; treat it as a test tool, not production infrastructure.
stories.chip: Checked on Amazon's own post
src: About Amazon: how agents built AWS Emulator
stories.short: AWS released AWS Emulator, a free tool that runs AWS services locally for testing. Amazon says every line was written by thousands of autonomous AI agents that write tests and fix bugs with no human code review. The code is public on GitHub under a CC0 licence.

stat.label: of the code written by AI agents

stories.title: Google DeepMind announces AlphaGenome 2, a DNA sequence model that predicts how sequences and genetic variants affect gene activity in hundreds of specific human cell types, linking single-cell biology to human genetics to find the cellular drivers of disease
stories.h: DeepMind's AlphaGenome 2 predicts how gene variants act cell by cell
stories.ticker: DeepMind's AlphaGenome 2 predicts variant effects across hundreds of human cell types
stories.body:
Google DeepMind announced AlphaGenome 2, its next DNA sequence model. Where last year's AlphaGenome predicted how DNA variants affect gene regulation, version 2 predicts how sequences and variants change gene activity in hundreds of specific human cell types, bridging single-cell maps such as the Human Cell Atlas and human genetics. DeepMind pitches it as a way to find which cells drive a disease, and published a paper alongside.

So what: most disease-linked variants sit outside genes and act in particular cell types; a model that says which cells a variant affects narrows drug-target searches. Watch for access terms and independent benchmarks before treating the claims as settled.
stories.chip: Checked on DeepMind's announcement
stories.short: Google DeepMind announced AlphaGenome 2, a DNA model that predicts how genetic variants change gene activity in hundreds of specific human cell types. DeepMind says it helps find the cells that drive a disease; independent tests and access terms are still to come.

stories.title: IBM updates its quantum roadmap: a Nighthawk r3 processor with 520+ programmable qubits, two Nighthawk chips linked into a ~1,040-qubit system available in 2027 (down from a plan to link nine), error-corrected machines targeted before 2030, and gains from hardware qubit resets; Quantinuum separately upgrades RIKEN's machine and partners with SoftBank
stories.h: IBM plans a 1,040-qubit linked quantum system for 2027
stories.ticker: IBM: two linked Nighthawk chips, ~1,040 qubits, for users in 2027
stories.body:
At its Quantum Developer Conference, IBM updated its roadmap, Ars Technica reports. A new Nighthawk general-purpose processor version (r3) has over 500 programmable qubits (SiliconANGLE: 520, running 10,000 operations); IBM will link two of them (not nine, as planned) for about 1,040 qubits on offer in 2027, keeping the total qubit target. It still aims for error-corrected quantum computers before the decade is out, on a separate development track, and credits hardware-based qubit resets in September's chips for a performance jump. Separately, Quantinuum upgraded its machine at Japan's RIKEN and agreed to deploy with SoftBank in AI data centres (DCD, headline).

So what: this is Thursday's deep beat. Bigger, linked chips are steady progress, not code-breaking: banks' post-quantum migration timelines do not change, but the 'harvest now, decrypt later' risk keeps the deadline real.
stories.chip: Checked on Ars Technica; qubit-count detail from SiliconANGLE headline; Quantinuum from DCD headline
stories.short: IBM will offer a quantum system of two linked Nighthawk chips, about 1,040 qubits, in 2027, scaling back a plan to link nine chips but keeping its qubit target. It still aims for error-corrected machines before 2030. Quantinuum separately upgraded RIKEN's quantum computer and teamed up with SoftBank.

stories.title: Spain holds its first general strike in 14 years over housing and living costs: about 120,000 march in Madrid and 50,000+ in Barcelona, where masked groups clash with police; transport and public services are disrupted, 18 days before the 29 Nov general election
stories.h: Spain's first general strike in 14 years ends in Barcelona clashes
stories.ticker: Spain's first general strike in 14 years over housing; clashes in Barcelona
stories.body:
Spain's main unions held the country's first general strike in 14 years, over housing and the cost of living, the BBC reports. Some 120,000 people marched in Madrid and more than 50,000 in Barcelona, where masked groups burned bins, smashed windows and looted shops as police fired tear gas. Transport and public services were badly disrupted. UGT's Pepe Álvarez called turnout "massive". Spain votes in a general election on 29 November.

So what: housing costs are now an election-deciding issue in one of the euro area's fastest-growing economies. Spanish banks' mortgage books and any housing-tax or rent-control promises in the campaign are the things to watch.
stories.chip: Checked on BBC News
stories.short: Spain held its first general strike in 14 years over housing and living costs. About 120,000 marched in Madrid and over 50,000 in Barcelona, where masked groups clashed with police. Transport was disrupted. Spain votes in a general election on 29 November.

stories.title: AP calls Mississippi's Senate race for Democrat Scott Colom over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, a week after the 3 Nov midterms; he will be the state's first Black senator elected since 1874, adding to the Democrats' new majority
stories.h: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi's Senate seat
stories.ticker: AP calls Mississippi Senate race for Democrat Scott Colom
stories.body:
The Associated Press called Mississippi's US Senate race for Democrat Scott Colom, a district attorney, over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, just over a week after the election, Rolling Stone reports; he led by about 2,000 votes the day after polling and widened the margin. The Guardian notes he will be the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since 1874. Rolling Stone calls it the most shocking of the Democrats' midterm upsets, which included a statewide sweep in Texas.

So what: every extra Democratic Senate seat strengthens the incoming majority that will set crypto, bank-capital and AI rules from January.
stories.chip: Checked on Rolling Stone

stories.title: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is moved from his Georgetown home to a military base after Iran-linked threats, after a WSJ photo allowed his home to be geolocated; Treasury says he 'will not be deterred'
stories.h: Bessent moved to a military base after Iran-linked threats
stories.ticker: Treasury Secretary Bessent relocated to military base over Iran-linked threats
stories.body:
Scott Bessent, the US Treasury Secretary who leads the economic blockade of Iran, has been moved from his Washington home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, the BBC reports, citing CBS. A source said concern rose after a photo in the Wall Street Journal let his Georgetown home be geolocated. US intelligence has warned Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans, including officials. Treasury said Bessent "will not be deterred". France this week blamed Iran's Revolutionary Guards for sabotaging refrigeration controllers at about 700 shops.

So what: Iran's response to sanctions is reaching the officials and infrastructure behind them, in the US and Europe.
stories.chip: Checked on BBC News

stories.title: France blames an IRGC cyber unit, Shahid Kaveh (CyberAveng3rs), for the 11 Oct sabotage of refrigeration controllers at about 700 French retail sites: defrost settings were changed to high temperatures, spoiling food and causing at least 15 fires; Paris opens a judicial investigation, seeks arrest warrants and will push for EU sanctions
stories.h: France says Iran's Guards sabotaged fridges at 700 shops
stories.ticker: France blames IRGC unit for sabotaging fridge controllers at ~700 shops
stories.body:
The French government says a cyber unit of Iran's Revolutionary Guards, Shahid Kaveh (known through personas such as CyberAveng3rs), broke into refrigeration controllers at about 700 retail sites on the night of 11 October and set defrost temperatures high, spoiling food and causing at least 15 fires, The Hacker News reports. Paris prosecutors opened a judicial investigation into the unit's head and two deputies and requested international arrest warrants; the foreign ministry will summon Iran's ambassador and seek new EU sanctions.

So what: internet-exposed building controls are now a state target in Europe, not just the US. Retail lenders and insurers should expect claims and questions on operational-technology security.
stories.chip: Checked on The Hacker News; NYT and Insurance Journal headlines

stories.title: New York lawmakers propose RAISE Act 2.0: fines of up to $1M a day for a first frontier-AI safety violation and $3M a day for later ones, coverage of any developer spending over $1B on models in three years, annual outside safety audits, quarterly reports on AI-run research and officer certification
stories.h: New York proposes $3m-a-day fines for frontier AI safety breaches
stories.ticker: New York RAISE Act 2.0 would fine AI labs up to $3M a day
stories.body:
A New York bill called RAISE Act 2.0 would fine frontier AI developers by the day: up to $1 million a day for a first safety violation and $3 million a day for later ones (up to $90M over 30 days), PYMNTS reports. It would cover any developer that spent over $1 billion on its models over three years and require annual outside safety audits, quarterly reports on research run by AI, and a senior officer's certification of filings. Governor Hochul this week also launched what Politico calls the first state AI testing programme (not opened).

So what: with Democrats taking Congress, state rules like New York's are likely to set the bar that federal law then copies.
stories.chip: Checked on PYMNTS (summary); bill text not opened

stories.title: Gartner forecasts AI will create 10.6M jobs and eliminate 8.9M by 2030, a net gain of 1.7M; in asset-intensive industries +6.4M/-6M (0.4% of workers), while ~70% of the tech workforce is highly exposed but the sector gains 1.9M and loses 0.4M
stories.h: Gartner: AI to create 1.7 million more jobs than it cuts by 2030
stories.ticker: Gartner: AI creates 10.6M jobs and removes 8.9M by 2030
stories.body:
Gartner forecasts AI will create 10.6 million jobs and remove 8.9 million by 2030, a net gain of 1.7 million, Insurance Business reports. In asset-intensive industries (the largest share of jobs) it expects 6.4M created and 6M eliminated, with losses hitting 0.4% of workers. Nearly 70% of the technology workforce is highly exposed, yet Gartner expects the sector to add 1.9M and lose 0.4M. In Australia, CNA reports companies face 'AI washing' accusations after job cuts and offshoring.

So what: a forecast, not data. It is useful mainly as a counterweight to cut-heavy narratives when boards set AI headcount targets.
stories.chip: Checked on Insurance Business (summary of Gartner's forecast)

stories.title: Cyber insurer Cowbell will launch a standalone AI liability policy for US SMEs in January 2027, built around an 'AI incident' trigger that combines first-party losses and third-party liability from agents that move money, file documents or deal with customers, sold via wholesale brokers on a non-admitted basis
stories.h: Cowbell launches insurance for mistakes made by AI agents
stories.ticker: Cowbell to sell standalone AI-agent liability cover to US SMEs from Jan 2027
stories.body:
Cowbell, a California cyber insurer for small and mid-sized firms, will launch Cowbell AI liability insurance in January 2027: a standalone policy for agentic AI that executes tasks, moves money, files documents and talks to customers without a human approving each step, Insurance Business reports. Cover is triggered by a defined 'AI incident' and combines first-party losses with third-party liability. It fills a gap left as ISO's CG 40 47 endorsement lets carriers exclude generative-AI injury and damage from general liability. Separately, Insurance Business reports banks are seeking credit-insurance cover for a surge in AI-related lending.

So what: a priced market for agent errors is forming. Banks offering agent payments to small businesses will want to know whether their clients' losses are insured, and by whom.
stories.chip: Checked on Insurance Business

stories.title: ECB board member Piero Cipollone urges EU negotiators to agree the digital euro regulation by year-end, warning a delay could push back a possible 2029 first issuance and deepen Europe's dependence on foreign payment providers
stories.h: ECB warns digital euro could slip past 2029 without a deal this year
stories.ticker: ECB: agree digital euro law by year-end or 2029 launch could slip
stories.body:
Piero Cipollone of the ECB's Executive Board told the European Parliament's economic committee that EU negotiators should reach a deal on the digital euro regulation by year-end, Cointelegraph reports. The ECB aims to be ready for a first issuance in 2029 if the law passes this year; "a delay in adoption could instead postpone the introduction," he said, warning of deeper dependence on foreign payment providers. The Governing Council decides on issuance only after the law passes.

So what: for euro-area banks the timeline drives spending on wallets, holding limits and deposit outflow planning; a slip buys time but prolongs uncertainty.
stories.chip: Checked on Cointelegraph

stories.title: India: equity mutual-fund inflows fall 14% in October to ₹33,000 crore (AMFI) after the Nifty hit its lowest since April 2025 early in the month; the 10-year bond has its worst day in a month on the US Treasury rout, while the rupee closes at 93.69, its strongest since April, on foreign equity inflows
stories.h: India's fund inflows cool as US yields hit bonds; rupee firms
stories.ticker: India equity MF inflows -14% in Oct; 10-year bond worst day in a month; rupee 93.69
stories.body:
Net inflows into Indian equity mutual funds fell 14% in October to ₹33,000 crore (~$3.5bn) from ₹38,310 crore, AMFI data show (Bloomberg via Mint), as investors grew wary of small and mid caps after the Nifty 50 hit its lowest since April 2025 early in the month; debt funds took in ₹1.13 trillion. On Wednesday India's 10-year bond had its worst day in a month as US Treasuries sold off after hot US inflation (Reuters via ET), while the rupee closed at 93.69 per dollar, its strongest since April, on foreign buying of Indian stocks.

So what: domestic SIP money has been the cushion against foreign selling; if it cools while US yields rise, Indian banks' bond portfolios and treasury income feel it first.
stories.chip: Checked on Mint (Bloomberg) and Economic Times (Reuters)

stories.title: Benchmark Mineral Intelligence: global EV sales rise 8% y/y in October to 2.09M; Europe 510,000 (+36%, battery-electric +49%), China 1.14M (-12%), North America 0.13M (+24%, its first rise of 2026); 17.5M year to date (+5%)
stories.h: Europe's electric car sales jump 49% as China's fall
stories.ticker: Oct EV sales: global +8%, Europe BEV +49%, China -12%
stories.body:
Drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide in October, up 8% year on year, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence data reported by Electrek. Europe sold 510,000 (+36%), with battery-electric cars up 49%; China fell 12% to 1.14M; North America rose 24% to 0.13M, its first year-on-year rise in 2026; the rest of the world grew 85%. Year-to-date sales are 17.5M, up 5%.

So what: Europe and emerging markets now carry EV growth while China cools, which matters for auto-loan books and battery-metal prices.
stories.chip: Checked on Electrek (Benchmark data)

stories.title: Certificate authority eMudhra revokes eight more intermediate CA certificates (16 in total) after finding a buggy custom Python script used in April 2025 to move CA private keys between HSM vendors weakened key handling; eight earlier keys were so weak they could be recovered almost instantly
stories.h: eMudhra revokes 16 CA certificates over a key-handling script bug
stories.ticker: eMudhra revokes 8 more intermediate CA certificates (16 total)
stories.body:
eMudhra, an Indian certificate authority, revoked eight more intermediate CA certificates, bringing the total to 16, BleepingComputer reports. Its incident report says both sets were affected by a custom Python script used in April 2025 to transfer CA private keys between hardware security modules from different vendors after new hardware was delayed; a bug weakened the keys, and the first eight were so weak anyone could recover them almost instantly.

So what: certificates chained to these intermediates stop working; Indian banks and government services that use eMudhra for TLS or document signing should check their chains.
stories.chip: Checked on BleepingComputer

stories.title: Total stablecoin supply falls about $14B in 30 days, the fastest drop since June 2022, as bitcoin hovers near $74K and ETF investors sell
stories.h: Stablecoin supply falls $14bn in a month, most since 2022
stories.ticker: Stablecoin supply down $14B in 30 days, fastest since June 2022
stories.body:
Total stablecoin supply has fallen about $14 billion in 30 days, the fastest decline since June 2022, Crypto Briefing reports. Bitcoin hovered near $74,000 (Cointelegraph) as ETF investors kept selling (CryptoSlate).

So what: stablecoins are the cash leg of crypto; a shrinking float usually means money leaving the market, which banks launching custody and tokenised products will feel in volumes.
stories.chip: Checked on Crypto Briefing; data source not named in the article

stories.title: Tether AI Research (QVAC) introduces BotPsy, an on-device personal assistant built on a 0.8B-parameter agentic language model, pitched as a private, self-hosted alternative to frontier cloud models for routine tasks
stories.h: Tether shows a sub-billion-parameter agent that runs on the phone
stories.ticker: Tether AI's BotPsy: on-device assistant on a 0.8B agentic model
stories.body:
Tether AI Research, the stablecoin issuer's research arm (QVAC), published BotPsy on the Hugging Face blog: an on-device personal assistant built on a 0.8-billion-parameter agentic language model. The authors argue routine tasks do not need frontier models, that cloud models' costs and access can change without notice, and that small specialised agents can match them on narrow jobs while keeping data on the device.

So what: small agent models running locally are the privacy-friendly route for customer-facing assistants in regulated firms; benchmark claims still need independent checks.
stories.chip: Checked on the Hugging Face blog post

stories.title: A builder's AI agents analysed NASA lidar data and found a Maya site in Mexico missing from INAH's register in under 72 hours, from idea to a reply from the Mexican government; an update says archaeologists had already mapped it (Estrada-Belli et al. 2025), so it was a rediscovery the agents missed in the literature
stories.h: AI agents found a Maya site in lidar data, then learned it was known
stories.ticker: Builder's AI agents (re)discover Maya site in NASA lidar in 72 hours
stories.body:
Pietro Miotti describes how his AI agents analysed NASA lidar data and flagged a Maya site in Mexico that was not in the register of the national heritage institute (INAH), going from a passing idea to an official government reply in under 72 hours. An update on 11 November says archaeologists had in fact mapped it in a 2025 paper; the agents missed it while reviewing the literature. The post topped Hacker News with 917 points.

So what: an idea worth copying: agents that sift public sensor data for anomalies, then check them against registers. The miss is the lesson, too: the literature check is the weak step.
stories.chip: Checked on the author's post

stories.title: French Open champion Mirra Andreeva, 19, wins 11 games in a row to beat world No 2 Aryna Sabalenka 6-4 6-0 and reach the WTA Finals semi-finals; Elina Svitolina beats Karolina Muchova
stories.h: Andreeva wins 11 straight games to rout Sabalenka at WTA Finals
stories.ticker: Andreeva beats Sabalenka 6-4 6-0 to reach WTA Finals semis
stories.body:
Mirra Andreeva, the 19-year-old French Open champion, came from 4-1 down to win 11 games in a row and beat world number two Aryna Sabalenka 6-4 6-0, reaching the last four at the WTA Finals, BBC Sport reports. Elina Svitolina beat Karolina Muchova.

So what: Andreeva joins Linda Noskova in the semi-finals.
stories.chip: Checked on BBC Sport

stories.title: Tim Peters (1952-2026), the Python core developer who wrote 'The Zen of Python' and the Timsort algorithm, has died, the Python community announces
stories.h: Tim Peters, author of the Zen of Python and Timsort, dies
stories.ticker: Python core developer Tim Peters (Zen of Python, Timsort) dies
stories.body:
The Python community announced the death of Tim Peters (1952-2026) in an 'In Memoriam' post on discuss.python.org. Peters, a long-time Python core developer, wrote 'The Zen of Python' and created Timsort, the sorting algorithm later adopted by Java, Android and other platforms. The news drew 817 points on Hacker News.

So what: Timsort runs inside much of the world's software, including bank systems on the JVM.
stories.chip: Checked on the Python Software Foundation's Discourse forum

stories.title: Nvidia's board meets to decide Jensen Huang's future after the WSJ reports it is preparing to oust him and the NYT reports a second relationship, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's VP of healthcare, who reports to him; Bloomberg says the board is working with an outside firm on successors and weighs an interim CEO; shares fall ~8% after hours (about 20% since the scandal began); no decision announced as of publication
stories.h: Nvidia board weighs ousting Jensen Huang as a second affair is reported
stories.sub: The WSJ says the board is preparing to remove its founder; shares fell about 8% after hours, and no decision had been announced by publication.
stories.ticker: Nvidia board meets on Huang's future after WSJ ouster report; shares -8% after hours
stories.update: Escalated: the WSJ reports the board is preparing to oust Huang; the NYT reports a second relationship with VP Kimberly Powell; the board met on Wednesday; shares fell ~8% after hours
stories.body:
Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to weigh the future of Jensen Huang, its only chief executive in 33 years, the FT reports (text via Ars Technica), after the Wall Street Journal said the board was preparing to oust him. The New York Times reported a second relationship, with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice-president of healthcare, who reports to him. Bloomberg says the board is working with an outside firm to identify replacements and may name an interim CEO. Nvidia declined to comment to the NYT; on Sunday the board had backed Huang after he admitted an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a customer whom US intelligence believes was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. Shares fell about 8% after hours (Business Insider); CoreWeave, Supermicro, Micron and TSMC fell 2-5%. No decision had been announced by publication.

So what: Nvidia is the largest weight in global equity indexes and the centre of AI supply. A forced exit with no succession plan hits index funds, AI-infrastructure credit and the chip-export debate in Washington at once. Watch for a board statement before the US open.
stories.chip: Checked on the FT's report (via Ars Technica), Business Insider and The Japan Times; WSJ, NYT and Bloomberg seen only as headlines
stories.brief: Three reports landed within hours on Wednesday evening, US time: the WSJ said the board was preparing to remove Huang and would meet as soon as that day; the NYT, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, said he had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, an 18-year Nvidia veteran who reports to him; and Bloomberg said the board was working with an outside firm on possible successors and weighing a temporary CEO. The FT confirmed the board meeting. Nvidia has made no statement on the Powell report. On Sunday the board said it backed Huang while former US Attorney Joon Kim of Wachtell investigates whether he was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
facts: Board meets on whether to remove CEO Jensen Huang
WSJ ouster report; NYT report of a second affair, with VP Kimberly Powell
Outside search firm; possible interim CEO (Bloomberg)
Nvidia down about 8% after hours; about 20% since the scandal began
stories.impactWho: Index and AI-sector investors, Nvidia's customers and suppliers, lenders to AI-infrastructure firms, and US chip-export policymakers
stories.short: Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to decide whether to remove Jensen Huang after the WSJ said it was preparing to oust him and the NYT reported a second affair, with an executive who reports to him. Bloomberg says a successor search firm is involved. Shares fell about 8% after hours. No decision yet.

stories.title: Saudi Arabia says debris from two Houthi ballistic missiles intercepted over the Mecca region fell in several places; it also intercepted cruise missiles aimed at Riyadh and drones; the Houthis deny targeting Mecca and say they hit a Yanbu pumping station; Brent jumps ~3% to ~$94 as Iran denies talks with Washington, then settles below $93; Iran's Ghalibaf says Hormuz will 'never return' to its pre-war status
stories.h: Houthi missiles over Mecca as Iran denies talks; oil bounces
stories.ticker: Saudi intercepts missiles over Mecca region; Brent back near $93 as Iran denies talks
stories.update: Escalated: Houthi missiles and drones aimed at Riyadh and the Mecca region; strike on Yanbu pumping station; Brent rebounds from below $90 to ~$93
stories.body:
Saudi Arabia's civil defence said debris from two ballistic missiles intercepted over the Mecca region fell in several places, Reuters reports (via ThePrint). Earlier the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed three cruise missiles headed for Riyadh, two drones aimed at Mecca and southern areas and two more missiles (Reuters via Cyprus Mail). The Houthis denied targeting Mecca and said they hit a pumping station at Yanbu, the Red Sea hub that lets Saudi crude avoid the blocked Strait of Hormuz. Brent jumped about 3% to ~$94 when Iran denied any talks with Washington (OilPrice), then settled below $93 (Bloomberg via Mint). Iran's top negotiator Ghalibaf told Al Jazeera Hormuz will "never return" to its pre-war status and that Iran and Oman will oversee it. Saudi output rose 26% in October.

So what: yesterday's dip below $90 did not last. Attacks on the routes that bypass Hormuz keep a risk premium in oil, and with it in inflation and the case for a December Fed hike.
stories.chip: Checked on Reuters (via ThePrint and Cyprus Mail), OilPrice, Mint and Al Jazeera
stories.short: Saudi Arabia intercepted Houthi missiles and drones aimed at Riyadh and the Mecca region; debris fell near Mecca. The Houthis deny targeting the holy city and say they hit the Yanbu export hub. Brent rebounded towards $93 as Iran denied talks with the US.

stories.title: Notion confirms the Fireworks AI breach exposed Notion AI chat transcripts in a small number of workspaces, from the dataset behind its Insights admin feature (now disabled); Notion cut traffic to Fireworks, deleted its data there and halted training runs by 3 Nov after a 2 Nov alert, and Fireworks confirmed customer data access on 8 Nov
stories.h: Notion confirms Fireworks breach exposed AI chat transcripts
stories.ticker: Notion: Fireworks breach exposed Notion AI chat transcripts; Insights disabled
stories.update: Notion's own disclosure: transcripts from its Insights dataset in a small number of workspaces were exposed; Insights disabled, Fireworks traffic cut
stories.body:
Notion disclosed that the breach at its AI infrastructure provider Fireworks AI exposed Notion AI chat transcripts in a small number of workspaces, BleepingComputer reports. The transcripts came from the dataset behind Insights, a feature that shows admins how teams use AI, which Notion has now disabled. Fireworks alerted Notion on 2 November about an exposed dataset it said held only synthetic test data; Notion cut traffic to Fireworks, deleted all its data from Fireworks' systems and halted training runs by 3 November; Fireworks confirmed on 8 November that customer data had been accessed. Fireworks runs some open-weight models in Notion AI.

So what: usage-analytics features quietly keep copies of prompts. Ask SaaS vendors which sub-processors hold chat logs, for how long, and for what features.
stories.chip: Checked on BleepingComputer
stories.short: Notion confirmed that the breach at its AI provider Fireworks exposed Notion AI chat transcripts in a small number of workspaces, taken from the data behind its admin Insights feature. Notion cut off Fireworks, deleted its data there and disabled Insights.

stories.title: Two days of US-Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi end with Russia and Ukraine agreeing in principle to a major prisoner exchange, their first negotiations in nine months; US mediators say a lack of trust and differences on territory remain
stories.h: Abu Dhabi talks end with a prisoner swap deal but no territory deal
stories.ticker: Russia and Ukraine agree prisoner swap in Abu Dhabi; territory gap remains
stories.update: Talks ended Wednesday with a prisoner exchange agreed in principle; US says trust and territory still block a deal
stories.body:
Russian and Ukrainian negotiators agreed in principle to a major prisoner exchange at two days of talks in Abu Dhabi that ended on Wednesday, their first negotiations in nine months, Reuters reports (via The Japan Times); numbers are still to be set. US mediators, including Jared Kushner, said differences remain on major issues, including territory, and that a lack of trust is holding talks back.

So what: a humanitarian step, not a ceasefire; European defence and reconstruction plans stay on their current track.
stories.chip: Checked on The Japan Times (Reuters)
